title: General Principles of Pharmacology (PHA 301)
description: Pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion), pharmacodynamics, dose–response, adverse drug reactions, interactions and drug development.

topics.title: Drug Absorption and Bioavailability
topics.summary: Routes, membrane transport of drugs, ionisation, first-pass metabolism and bioavailability.

notes.b: Most drugs cross membranes by passive diffusion of the un-ionised, lipid-soluble form. Ionisation depends on the drug's pKa and the pH of the environment (Henderson–Hasselbalch): weak acids (aspirin) are more un-ionised in acidic environments; weak bases (morphine, amphetamine) are more un-ionised in alkaline environments. 'Ion trapping' is used in poisoning — alkalinising urine enhances excretion of weak acids such as salicylates. Absorption is affected by formulation, gut motility, food, blood flow and surface area; most oral absorption occurs in the small intestine.
k: Weak acids absorbed better in acid pH

notes.b: Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of an administered dose reaching the systemic circulation unchanged; it is 100% for intravenous drugs. Oral drugs absorbed from the gut pass through the portal vein and liver first; extensive first-pass (presystemic) metabolism reduces bioavailability (e.g. glyceryl trinitrate, propranolol, lidocaine, morphine). Sublingual, rectal (partly), transdermal and parenteral routes avoid or reduce first-pass metabolism. Bioavailability is calculated from the area under the plasma concentration–time curve (AUC oral ÷ AUC IV). Bioequivalence studies compare generic and innovator products.

q: Drugs cross cell membranes most readily when they are:
Lipid-soluble un-ionised molecules diffuse through membranes.
Aspirin (a weak acid) is mainly un-ionised in:
Weak acids are un-ionised at low pH.
Excretion of salicylates in overdose is increased by:
Alkaline urine ionises and traps salicylate in the tubule.
The bioavailability of an intravenous drug is:
The whole dose enters the circulation.
Glyceryl trinitrate is given sublingually because it:
Is inactive orally due to extensive first-pass metabolism
Comparing areas under the curve gives the fraction absorbed unchanged.
Most oral drug absorption takes place in the:
The small intestine has the largest surface area.
Studies comparing a generic drug with the original brand for rate and extent of absorption are:
Bioequivalence confirms comparable AUC and Cmax.

topics.title: Distribution, Metabolism and Excretion
topics.summary: Volume of distribution, protein binding, phase I and II metabolism, enzyme induction and renal excretion.

notes.b: Volume of distribution (Vd) = amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma concentration; it is a theoretical volume. Drugs highly bound to plasma proteins (warfarin, phenytoin — to albumin) or confined to plasma have small Vd; lipid-soluble drugs concentrated in tissues (chloroquine, digoxin, amiodarone) have very large Vd. Only free (unbound) drug is active and can be metabolised or excreted; displacement from protein binding and low albumin increase free drug. The blood–brain barrier excludes many polar drugs; the placenta allows most lipid-soluble drugs to reach the fetus.

The liver makes drugs more water-soluble. Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis — mainly cytochrome P450, especially CYP3A4) introduce or expose functional groups. Phase II reactions conjugate drugs with glucuronic acid, sulphate, acetyl (N-acetyltransferase — slow and fast acetylators of isoniazid), glutathione or glycine. Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, chronic alcohol, St John's wort) reduce levels of other drugs (e.g. contraceptive failure, reduced antiretroviral levels). Inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin/clarithromycin, ciprofloxacin, grapefruit juice, cimetidine, ritonavir) raise levels and toxicity. Kidneys excrete drugs by glomerular filtration, active tubular secretion (penicillin, blocked by probenecid) and reduced by passive reabsorption.
k: Phase I: CYP450; Phase II: conjugation

q: A drug with a very large volume of distribution is mainly:
Large Vd implies extensive tissue uptake (e.g. chloroquine).

topics.title: Pharmacokinetic Parameters and Dosing
topics.summary: Half-life, clearance, steady state, loading and maintenance doses, and zero-order kinetics.

notes.b: Clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. Elimination half-life t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL. Most drugs follow first-order kinetics: a constant fraction is eliminated per unit time, so t½ is constant. Some drugs follow zero-order (saturation) kinetics at usual or high doses: a constant amount is eliminated per unit time — ethanol, phenytoin and high-dose aspirin — so small dose increases may cause large rises in plasma levels. It takes about 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state with repeated dosing, and about 4–5 half-lives for a drug to be almost completely eliminated.

A loading dose rapidly achieves the target concentration: loading dose = target concentration × Vd (used for drugs with long half-lives, e.g. digoxin, amiodarone, loading doses of artemether–lumefantrine or quinine in severe malaria). The maintenance dose rate = target concentration × clearance, balancing elimination. In renal impairment, doses of renally cleared drugs (gentamicin, vancomycin, metformin, digoxin) must be reduced. Therapeutic drug monitoring is used for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, aminoglycosides, vancomycin).
k: Reduce renally cleared drugs in kidney disease
TDM for narrow therapeutic index drugs

topics.title: Pharmacodynamics: Receptors and Dose–Response
topics.summary: Drug targets, agonists and antagonists, potency and efficacy, therapeutic index and tolerance.

notes.b: Drugs act on receptors, enzymes, ion channels and transporters. Receptor types: ligand-gated ion channels (nicotinic, GABA-A — milliseconds), G-protein-coupled receptors (muscarinic, adrenergic, opioid — seconds), enzyme-linked receptors (insulin — minutes) and nuclear receptors (steroids, thyroid hormone — hours). An agonist binds and activates a receptor (affinity + intrinsic activity); a full agonist gives the maximal response; a partial agonist gives a submaximal response even at full occupancy and can antagonise full agonists (e.g. buprenorphine). An inverse agonist produces the opposite effect of an agonist. Antagonists have affinity but no efficacy: competitive (reversible) antagonists shift the dose–response curve to the right without reducing maximum (e.g. naloxone, atropine); irreversible/non-competitive antagonists reduce the maximum response (e.g. phenoxybenzamine).

Potency is the amount of drug needed to produce a given effect (EC50); efficacy is the maximum effect achievable (Emax) — clinically, efficacy usually matters more. The therapeutic index (TI) = TD50/ED50 (or LD50/ED50); a narrow TI (warfarin, digoxin, lithium, theophylline, aminoglycosides) demands careful dosing. Tolerance is reduced response with repeated use (opioids, nitrates, benzodiazepines); tachyphylaxis is rapid tolerance (ephedrine). Receptor down-regulation follows chronic agonist exposure; up-regulation follows chronic antagonist use (rebound hypertension/tachycardia on abrupt β-blocker withdrawal).

q: A drug that binds a receptor but produces no response and blocks the agonist is a/an:
Antagonists have affinity but no efficacy.

Buprenorphine is an example of a:

Ion channel opening changes membrane potential almost instantly.

topics.title: Adverse Drug Reactions, Interactions and Drug Development
topics.summary: Types of ADRs, pharmacovigilance, drugs in pregnancy, drug interactions and clinical trial phases.

notes.b: Type A (augmented) reactions are dose-related extensions of the drug's known pharmacology and are common and predictable (e.g. bleeding with warfarin, hypoglycaemia with insulin). Type B (bizarre) reactions are unpredictable and not dose-related, including allergy and idiosyncrasy (e.g. anaphylaxis to penicillin, Stevens–Johnson syndrome with sulphonamides or nevirapine, haemolysis with primaquine in G6PD deficiency). Other types: C (chronic — steroid-induced osteoporosis), D (delayed — teratogenesis, carcinogenesis), E (end-of-use — withdrawal), F (failure of therapy). Teratogens include thalidomide, isotretinoin, warfarin, valproate, phenytoin, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines and methotrexate. In Nigeria, suspected ADRs are reported to NAFDAC's pharmacovigilance centre using the yellow form or the Med Safety app.

Pharmacokinetic interactions alter absorption (antacids/iron chelating tetracyclines), protein binding, metabolism (inducers/inhibitors) or excretion. Pharmacodynamic interactions are additive, synergistic or antagonistic at the effect level (e.g. alcohol with benzodiazepines → respiratory depression; NSAIDs reduce the effect of antihypertensives). Drug development: preclinical studies (in vitro and animal); Phase I (small numbers of healthy volunteers — safety, pharmacokinetics); Phase II (small numbers of patients — efficacy and dosing); Phase III (large randomised controlled trials — confirm efficacy and safety before licensing); Phase IV (post-marketing surveillance — rare and long-term effects).
k: Phase III: large RCTs before approval
